newsitem.title: USA: US study knocks link between power lines, cancer.
newsitem.headline: US study knocks link between power lines, cancer.

text.p: Researchers studying health effects of electromagnetic fields concluded that power lines do not increase the risk of leukemia in children, according to a report released on Wednesday.

Unlike past studies, some of which have suggested a link between power lines and cancer, the new research directly measured electromagnetic fields in the home. Other studies simply estimated a child's exposure.

The new findings were to be published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine and came from a team led by Martha Linet of the National Cancer Institute in Bethesda, Maryland. The research was expected to allay fears that surfaced in 1979 when some scientists found a connection between cancer and the fields given off by power lines and electrical appliances.

The study financed by the NCI and the University of Minnesota's Children's Cancer Research Fund looked at 638 children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia and compared their living conditions with those of 620 youngsters without cancer.
They also had technicians directly measure electromagnetic fields in each child's home and former homes. The technicians did not know which homes had the leukemia patients.
Finally, researchers checked to see if the mother lived near power lines when she was pregnant.

Linet and her colleagues discovered that no matter how they measured a child's exposure to power line fields they did not find any evidence that the children with leukemia had been exposed to more electromagnetic energy than healthy children.
In an editorial journal deputy editor Edward Campion said the study may not put the controversy to rest but it should.

Although the concept of cancer-causing electromagnetic fields has sparked a lot of media attention, "in recent years several commissions and expert panels have concluded that there is no convincing evidence that high-voltage power lines are a health hazard or a cause of cancer," he said.

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common childhood cancer, afflicting about 2,000 children each year and killing 30 percent of them. Doctors know it can be caused by exposure to conventional radiation but otherwise the cause of the disease is unknown, nor is it known why the number of cases has increased 20 percent in 20 years, Campion said.

Because Earth itself has a stronger magnetic field than that under a high-voltage transmission line, he said, "it is sad that hundreds of millions of dollars have gone into studies that never had much promise of finding a way to prevent the tragedy of cancer in children."

Eighteen years of inconclusive and inconsistent studies "have produced considerable paranoia, but little insight and no prevention," Campion said. "It is time to stop wasting our research resources. We should redirect them to research that will be able to discover the true biologic causes of the leukemic clones that threaten the lives of children."
